concept.name: Parabolic advance
concept.definition: A chart formation in which an uptrend accelerates so that successive rallies steepen and the price path curves upward like a parabola, often with stair-step consolidations ('bases') beneath a curving trend line. It is interpreted as crowd-driven euphoria whose slope is mathematically unsustainable, so the pattern is used as a bearish-reversal framework: the signal is price breaking back below the curved trend line. It is an analytical hypothesis, not a proven predictive law.
concept.intuition: When each wave of buying has to be more frantic than the last just to keep the rally going, the move is feeding on itself; once the curve cracks, there is no orderly bid underneath.
concept.mechanics: Identify a prevailing bullish trend, locate a series of measured pullbacks, and draw a curving (parabolic) trend line beneath the pullback lows; as the slope steepens, each base forms higher and faster. The trade signal is a close beneath the curved trend line, with a stop above the pattern's upper extreme and targets set from the curve or via Fibonacci retracements. Parabolic moves frequently retrace a large share of the entire advance.
concept.failure_modes: Strong trends stay 'parabolic' far longer than seems possible, and repeatedly re-steepening curves generate false breakdown signals against powerful momentum; shorting early into euphoria is a classic account-killer. In rotating, trendless markets the curved-line construction has no meaning.
concept.misconceptions: That a steep rally must reverse immediately — the pattern only signals exhaustion risk, and the actionable event is the break of the curved trend line, not the steepness itself. It is also unrelated to Wilder's Parabolic SAR indicator despite the shared name.
concept.example: A currency pair rises in three accelerating waves, each pullback higher and shallower, tracing a curve beneath the lows; when price closes below the curve at 1.3595, a short is entered with a stop above the 1.3627 high.
